820.title: Elizabeth of Hungary
820.hook: a young noblewoman who spent her fortune on a hospital; legend says bread turned to roses
820.howItsDone: Catholics, Lutherans and Anglicans honor Elizabeth of Hungary, and among hospitals, charities and parishes named for her, some of them mark her feast day with bread or food for the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dominic's preachers, awake all night at an inn. Your line was to contemplate and to share. What did you take in, and who did you hand it to? Day eight hundred twenty.

A young woman is hurrying down from a castle with her cloak held closed. Underneath it is bread, a lot of it, for the hungry people waiting below. Someone stops her on the path. In some tellings it's her husband, in others a suspicious relative. What are you carrying? She can't hide it, so she opens the cloak. And what falls out, the legend says, is roses. That's the story people tell about Elizabeth of Hungary, a king's daughter who married into a noble German house. The roses are a legend. The bread is not. Today: the woman behind the roses.

Elizabeth was born to the royal family of Hungary and sent as a girl to the court of Thuringia, in Germany, to marry Louis, the son of its ruler, who later ruled there himself. The early accounts say the marriage was a loving one. They also say she was not a comfortable person to have at a royal table. She refused food she believed had been taken unjustly from the poor. In a time of hunger she gave out grain from the stores, and she went down to the sick herself. Then her husband died, away from home, on his way to a crusade. Her life changed fast. She left court. She took up a life of poverty, close to the Franciscans. With what she had left of her own fortune, she built a hospital at Marburg, and she worked in it: washing, feeding, sitting with people others avoided. Behind all this is a passage from the Gospel of Matthew. Jesus says that when the Son of man comes in his glory, the king will tell people, "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." When they ask when, he says that whatever they did for the least of his family, they did for him. Read in that light, feeding the hungry is not a hobby. In the Gospel's own terms, it is serving Christ. In the Greek of the Gospels, the word for bread is artos, the same word as in the prayer, give us this day our daily bread. And the roses? Readers take the legend in different ways. Some hear a miracle. Some hear a picture: what you give in secret becomes beautiful. Either way, the story keeps her as she was, caught on the path, holding bread for someone else.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER AT A GERMAN COURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one loaf. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who could use bread this week, in any form. A neighbor who's sick. A coworker who skips lunch. Someone at a shelter or food bank near you. Let one face or one place come to mind. Then picture yourself bringing it: the walk there, the handing over, nothing hidden. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Elizabeth. A king's daughter of Hungary who fed the hungry, served the sick at a hospital she built, and, legend says, carried bread that became roses.
Your line: bread into roses. Today, bring someone bread, real or otherwise: a meal, a coffee, a snack left on a desk. Day eight hundred twenty.

the early accounts say she would not eat it, even at a royal table.
after her husband died, she stayed at court

options: say it's nothing and keep walking.
open the cloak.
turn back to the castle.
fork.reveal: in the legend she opens the cloak, and roses fall out. in the history, the bread kept coming.

what it means: a king's daughter who fed the hungry, left court when widowed, and built and worked in a hospital.
what a scholar hears: the rose miracle appears in later tellings; the early accounts, from her confessor and her maids, focus on her giving and her hospital at Marburg.

821.title: The dumb ox
821.hook: Thomas Aquinas was so quiet at school they called him the dumb ox
821.tomorrow: Aquinas: it all seems like straw
821.howItsDone: Catholics honor Thomas Aquinas as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and his writings are studied in Catholic seminaries and universities and by readers of other churches too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elizabeth, with bread under her cloak. Your line was bread into roses. Who got bread from you? Day eight hundred twenty-one.

In a lecture hall in Cologne sits a big student who almost never speaks. He listens. He writes. He doesn't argue in class. The other students decide he must not be very bright, and they give him a nickname: the dumb ox. One classmate feels sorry for him and offers to go over the lessons with him. The big student says yes, thank you, and sits there while the classmate explains. Then the classmate gets tangled in a hard passage and can't find his way out. And the quiet one, gently, explains the whole thing, clearly, start to finish. The student is Thomas Aquinas, and today's word is the name they gave him.

Thomas had already paid a price to be in that room. He came from a noble Italian family that had other plans for him, and when he joined Dominic's preachers, the friars we met two days ago, his family stopped him on the road and kept him at home for a long time, trying to change his mind. They couldn't. So now here he is, in Cologne, studying under a famous teacher, Albert, later called Albert the Great. The story of what happened next comes from Thomas's early biographer, William of Tocco. Albert gives the class a hard question and has Thomas answer it in public. And he does, with such clarity that Albert turns to the room. You call him the dumb ox, Albert says. But this ox will one day bellow so loud that the whole world will hear. Notice what the quiet was. Not emptiness. Attention. He wasn't speaking because he was listening, all the way down. And notice how he took the classmate's offer: no correction, no showing off, just yes, thank you. The letter of James puts it plainly, in the King James Bible: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak." Thomas was swift to hear. Later he would write a great deal, and Christians still read him, argue with him and learn from him. But it started with a young man nobody thought much of, sitting in the back, listening. The loudest voice in the room is not always the one that understands.

Here's the practice: value a quiet person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone in your life who doesn't say much. At work, at the table, in a group chat where they only ever react with a thumbs up. Hold them in mind for a moment. What might they be noticing that the rest of you miss? What have they never been asked? If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, just let your respect for them grow a little. The bell holds the time.
Dumb ox. The nickname classmates gave Thomas Aquinas because he was quiet. His teacher Albert said the ox would one day bellow.
Your line: the ox will bellow. Today, ask the quietest person you meet one real question, and then wait for the whole answer. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

822.title: Aquinas: it all seems like straw
822.hook: after an experience at Mass he stopped writing, saying all his work seemed like straw
822.howItsDone: Catholic students and teachers still study the Summa Theologiae, and the story of the straw is told in retreats and sermons about the limits of words before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dumb ox, the quiet student in the back. Your line was the ox will bellow. Who did you ask a real question, and did you wait for the answer? Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Straw. That's the word he used. The quiet student has grown into a great teacher. For years he has been writing a vast work explaining the Christian faith, question by question, answer by answer, dictating to helpers. Then one morning in Naples he says Mass, and something happens. The sources never say what. Afterward he puts down his pen. He won't write. He won't dictate. His friend and companion, Reginald, begs him to go on. And Thomas gives him a strange answer. Today: Aquinas, and the straw.

The account comes from testimony gathered after his death, when the church was looking into his life. Reginald presses him: why stop now? And Thomas says, in effect: I can't. Everything I have written seems like straw to me, compared with what I have seen. That's the whole story. He never says what he saw. He doesn't explain it, write it up or teach it. The great work, the one people still call the Summa, is left unfinished. He dies not long after, on a journey. What do you do with that? First, notice what he did not say. He did not say his work was false. He did not say burn it. Straw is not poison. Straw is what grain grows on. It holds the wheat up, and then the harvest is gathered and the straw is left in the field. The church kept reading him, and still does. Second, notice where it happened: at Mass, in prayer, not at a desk. Thomas had spent his life using reason to speak about God, and he believed reason was a gift. But Paul had already said that our knowing has a limit: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Some readers hear in the straw a man who glimpsed the face. Some readers also wonder whether he was ill or worn out, and say both could be true at once. The sources don't settle it. What they leave us is a teacher who stopped talking, and left a silence where the rest of his book should be.
screen: `STRAW, COMPARED WITH WHAT I HAVE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop, and let silence speak. Settle, and breathe. Put down whatever you're holding, the phone, the pen, the plan for the next hour. For this minute, add no words of your own. No explaining. No commentary in your head, or as little as you can manage. When a thought comes, let it go by like a cart on a far road. If you pray, you can sit with a line from the prophet Habakkuk: let all the earth keep silence before him. If you don't, just let the quiet be full. The bell holds the time.
Aquinas. Thomas Aquinas, the teacher who explained the faith question by question, and then stopped writing, saying it all seemed like straw beside what he had seen.
Your line: all is straw. Today, when you catch yourself explaining something a third time, stop, and let a little silence do the work. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

pairs: Paul on the limit of knowing

823.title: Bonaventure's journey
823.hook: the Franciscan who saw every creature as a step toward God
823.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God slowly, often on retreat, and some practice prayerful walks in nature that follow its first steps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aquinas put down his pen and called it all straw. Your line was all is straw. Where did you let a little silence do the work? Day eight hundred twenty-three.

What would it take to see a sparrow as a staircase? A Franciscan friar named Bonaventure climbs a mountain in Italy called La Verna. It's the mountain where, the story goes, Francis had a vision near the end of his life: a fiery angel, a seraph, with six wings. Bonaventure has a heavy job by now. He leads the whole family of Franciscan brothers. He goes up, he says, looking for peace. And while he's there, thinking about Francis's vision, an idea comes to him that becomes a small book. Today's word is the journey he wrote down.

The book is called The Journey of the Mind into God. Bonaventure reads the six wings as six steps. The soul climbs, he says, like going up a ladder, and the first rungs are right under your feet: the things God made. A stone, a river, a sparrow. Each one, he says, carries a trace of the one who made it, the way a footprint in the sand tells you someone walked there. Then you climb inward, to your own mind, where he finds God's image. Then upward, beyond what the mind can hold. But it starts with creatures. Behind that idea is a line from Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James Bible: "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Francis is close behind this, the man whose song, a few days back, made the sun a brother. Bonaventure gives that love a map. Every creature is a step. Not a stopping place, not something to grab and keep, but a step on the way up. And he was, by the stories told about him, a humble climber. Tradition says that when messengers arrived to tell him the pope had made him a cardinal, they found him washing dishes. He asked them to hang the cardinal's hat on a tree until he finished. Whether or not that's how it went, it's the kind of story told about a man who saw holy things in ordinary places. A dish. A tree. A sparrow on a fence.
screen: `SEEN BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one creature as a step. Find one living thing you can see from where you are: a plant, a bird outside, a dog asleep, even your own hand. Settle, and breathe. Look at it as if it were the first of its kind you'd ever seen. Its color. How it moves, or rests. What it needs to stay alive. Then let your attention rise a little, past it, toward whatever made it, however you name that. If you pray, you can give thanks for this one creature. If you don't, just let the looking be thanks enough. The bell holds the time.
Bonaventure's journey. His book The Journey of the Mind into God: climbing from the things God made, inward to the mind, and upward to God.
Your line: every creature a step. Today, when a living thing catches your eye, a tree, a pigeon, a stranger's dog, pause on it for one breath before you walk on. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

pairs: a trace of the one who made it

824.title: The Beguines
824.hook: lay women living together to pray and serve in medieval cities, like Mechthild of Magdeburg
824.howItsDone: Some beguinages in Belgium and the Netherlands still stand and can be visited, and Christian lay communities today, women's and mixed, still live together to pray and serve their neighborhoods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonaventure's journey up the ladder of creatures. Your line was every creature a step. Which living thing stopped you for a breath? Day eight hundred twenty-four.

Inside a medieval city, behind a wall and a gate, there's a little town of its own. Small houses around a green. A chapel. A garden. Women coming back in the evening from nursing the sick, or sitting at a loom, or teaching children their letters. At night the gate closes, and the bell rings for prayer. These women are not nuns. They haven't taken vows for life. Some of them could leave tomorrow and marry. But for now they've chosen to live here, together, to pray and to work and to serve the city around them. Today's word is what people called them.

The Beguines grew up in the cities of what is now Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. They were lay women, ordinary Christians, who wanted the gospel life without entering a convent. They lived in shared houses or in walled courts called beguinages. They earned their own living with their hands. They cared for the sick and the dying, and they prayed together. Their picture of life together goes back to the first Christians in Jerusalem, described in the Acts of the Apostles, in the King James Bible: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." The Greek word for in common there is koina. One Beguine became a writer. Mechthild of Magdeburg lived as a Beguine in that German city, and she wrote a book called The Flowing Light of the Godhead. She wrote it in German, the language of the street, not in Latin. It's full of love talk between the soul and God, bold and tender. In one passage she says, in effect, that a fish can't drown in water and a bird can't sink in the air, and the soul is made to live in God the same way. Not everyone was comfortable with women living like this, outside the usual rules, praying and writing in their own words. Church leaders at times grew suspicious, and some Beguines were investigated or condemned. Mechthild herself, late in life, went to live with nuns at a convent called Helfta. But the beguinages lasted, and you can still walk through some of them today. Women, together, in the middle of the city.

Here's the practice: serve with neighbors. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who live nearest you, on your street, in your building, in your town. Not one at a time, but together. Is there one thing you could do alongside them, not just for them? A cleanup. A meal train. Checking on the older neighbor together. Let one idea come, and keep it small. If you pray, you can hold your street in prayer. If you don't, just hold the faces you know there. The bell holds the time.
The Beguines. Lay women in medieval cities who lived together, without lifelong vows, to pray, work with their hands and serve the sick.
Your line: women together. Today, notice who in your life does the quiet caring work, and do one piece of it with them, side by side. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

825.title: Dante's journey
825.hook: midway through life's journey, lost in a dark wood, Dante is led by love through hell, purgatory and heaven
825.carry: the love that moves the sun
825.howItsDone: Christians and other readers take up Dante's Divine Comedy as poetry and as a spiritual journey, and some churches and reading groups go through it slowly, a canto at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beguines, living side by side behind a city gate. Your line was women together. Whose quiet caring work did you share? Day eight hundred twenty-five.

In the middle of the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood, for the straight way was lost. That's how a long Christian poem begins, put into plain English. A man, halfway through his life, wakes up lost. He doesn't know how he got there. The wood is wild and thick, and he can't find the path. He sees a hill with sunlight on it and tries to climb, and wild animals drive him back down. He is stuck. And then someone appears to help him. The man is the poet Dante, writing about himself, and today's word is the road he takes out.

The poem is known as the Divine Comedy. The help that comes to Dante in the wood is the ghost of Virgil, an old Roman poet, sent because a woman named Beatrice, whom Dante loved and who has died, asked for him. So the journey starts with love reaching down into the dark. Virgil leads Dante down through hell, where people are stuck forever in the shape of their choices. Then up a mountain, purgatory, where souls are being healed and made ready, climbing slowly, even singing. Then Beatrice herself guides him up through the heavens. The way out of the dark wood isn't straight up the sunny hill. It goes down first, and only then up. The poem is honest about pain. In heaven, Dante's ancestor tells him what's coming in his real life: he'll be driven out of his city, his Florence. He'll learn, the ancestor says, how salty another man's bread tastes, and how hard it is to climb another man's stairs. And then the last line. At the very end, Dante sees God, and he can't describe it. All he can say is that his desire and will were turned, like a wheel, by what he calls, in the Italian, "l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle." The love that moves the sun and the other stars. The poem began in a dark wood. It ends at the center of everything, with love. Christians read the poem in different ways, as a story, as a map of the soul, as a vision. Its first and last lines are a journey's two ends.

Here's the practice: name where you are in your journey. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: where am I right now? In a dark wood, not sure of the path? Going down, through something hard? Climbing slowly, being healed? Or somewhere bright? There's no wrong answer, and you don't have to fix it. Just name it, honestly, in a word or two. Then ask: who has been my Virgil, someone who helped me find the way? If you pray, you can bring that place and that person to God. If you don't, just hold them both for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Dante's journey. A poet lost in a dark wood, led by love down through hell, up the mountain of purgatory, and into heaven.
Your line: the love that moves the sun. Today, step outside once and look at the sun, or the sky where it is, and say the line to yourself. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

826.title: Palamas and the uncreated light
826.hook: on Mount Athos, monks praying the Jesus Prayer say they see the light of Tabor
826.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians, and some Catholics and Protestants, pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a prayer rope, and Orthodox churches keep a Sunday in Lent in memory of Gregory Palamas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dante's journey, from a dark wood to the love that moves the sun. Did you look up at the sky and say the line? Day eight hundred twenty-six.

Night on Mount Athos, a rocky peninsula in Greece, home to monks. In a small cell, a monk sits on a low stool, head bowed, eyes down. He is breathing slowly. With each breath he says a short prayer, the same one, over and over: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Hours go by. And some of these monks say that, in the stillness, they see light. Not a lamp. Not the moon. A light they say is God's own, the same light the disciples saw on Mount Tabor. Others laughed at them. Today's word is what the monks were doing.

Hesychasm. When Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, to "study to be quiet," the Greek verb he uses is from the same family: hesychazo, to be still. Hesychasts are the people of stillness. Their prayer, the Jesus Prayer, grows out of cries in the Gospels: the tax collector's "God be merciful to me a sinner," and the blind man calling, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Said slowly, with the breath. And the light? They point to the Transfiguration. Jesus takes three disciples up a mountain, tradition says Tabor, and there, Matthew writes, "his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." The monks say that light can still be seen. A learned man named Barlaam mocked them. God can't be seen with bodily eyes, he said. Whatever you're seeing, it's not God. A monk of Athos, Gregory Palamas, answered him. His answer turns on a distinction. God's essence, what God is in himself, is beyond every creature, forever. But God's energies, his life, his grace, his light, are truly God too, uncreated, and God gives them. So a person can really share in God's light without swallowing up God's mystery. Church councils in Constantinople sided with Palamas, and Orthodox Christians honor him as a saint. Western churches have read his ideas in different ways, and theologians still discuss them. For the people of stillness, the quiet was never empty. It was a cell kept ready for light.
screen: `HAVE MERCY ON ME, WITH THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a light in darkness. If you can, dim the room, and light a candle, or turn on one small lamp, or open your phone's screen to a blank white page and set it down. Settle, and breathe slowly. Let your eyes rest on the light without staring hard. Breathe in, breathe out. If you pray, you can say the old prayer of the monks with the breath, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. If you don't, let the breath be the prayer and the light be enough. The bell holds the time.
Hesychasm. Stillness: a way of prayer from the Christian East, the Jesus Prayer said with the breath, defended by Gregory Palamas.

Your line: the light of tabor. Look back over this week's seven days and pick the one that gave you light. Tonight, before you turn off the last lamp, sit with it for a breath. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

hesychasm means stillness
the people of stillness, from the same Greek family as Paul's study to be quiet.

fork.setup: you're Gregory Palamas. a learned man says the monks of Athos can't be seeing God's light, because God can't be seen. how do you answer?
options: agree, and tell the monks to stop.
say God's essence is beyond us, but God's energies, his light, are truly God and truly given.
say the monks see God's essence directly.
fork.reveal: Palamas distinguishes God's essence, beyond every creature, from God's energies, uncreated and truly shared. councils in Constantinople sided with him.

original.note: Greek: stillness, quiet. the stillness the hesychasts sought in prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks who meditate and imagine light.
what it means: the people of stillness pray the Jesus Prayer with the breath, and say they see the same light as at the Transfiguration.
what a scholar hears: Palamas's Triads against Barlaam: the distinction of God's essence and uncreated energies, upheld by councils in Constantinople.

sources.ref: Gregory Palamas, Triads in Defense of the Holy Hesychasts
